newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major relishes campaign rough and tumble.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major relishes campaign rough and tumble.

text.p: The louder the hecklers heckled, the broader grew John Major's smile.
Opponents seemed to outnumber blue-rosetted Conservatives in the 500-strong crowd that greeted the prime minister on Friday in the market square of Norwich in eastern England.
"Go home Tories!" "Just three more weeks, John!" "You're talking crap, John!"

A half-eaten sandwich was even hurled along with the insults, but they all bounced off harmlessly as Major kept the promise he made when he called the election for May 1 that the campaign would be gruelling but also fun.
Aides said later that Major was visibly fired up after the encounter. "I love it when they're out there shouting," he told one of them.
Twenty points behind the opposition Labour party in the opinion polls, Major has little to lose and has been throwing himself into the campaign with evident relish.
Labour leader Tony Blair, by contrast, has been criticised for an over-cautious, sanitised campaign designed to protect his poll lead but which risks turning off voters by dehumanising him.

Major, in a mocking allusion to the "New Labour New Britain" slogan, had earlier taunted Blair's aides for keeping him out of the way as if he was the plague "or new Black Death, as no doubt they would call it".

He returned to the attack in Norwich. "This election is starting to come alive and the more it becomes alive the less the Labour party will be able to hide their leader and their policies," he said to cries of "Bollocks!" and "Rubbish!"

Major's needling is finding an echo in the press. Writing in The Times newspaper, Matthew Parris railed against Labour "cabalists" who he said had surrounded their leader by a wall of glass to control all contact with the public.

Parris, a former Conservative member of parliament, recalled how former prime minister Margaret Thatcher grew distant with time and lost all sense of humour. "That is how she ended. It is no way for Mr Blair to start," he wrote.

"We need a visible symbol that he has broken the grip of his minders -- scorned them even. We need him to show he is not afraid of them, not afraid of us, not afraid of argument, not afraid of the unrehearsed," Parris added.
The left-leaning Guardian was also critical of what it called an uptight, hesitant Labour campaign so far, with Blair unprepared for aggressive challenges and afraid to take risks.

"There is too much calculation and not enough spontaneity. There seems to be an instinct of defensiveness when an instinct of confidence would better catch the moment," the paper said in an editorial.

Blair could do worse than take tips from Major, who knows how to turn heckling to his advantage. When one man shouted "What about the homeless?" Major seized the chance to explain how Conservatives planned to force Labour-run councils to sell empty homes.
It was a good end to a good week.
"Very good to see you all here. This is what electioneering should be about," he shouted cheerfully before boarding his battle bus for the next stop.
